summary: Outlines needs and requirements for a protocol to control distributed speech processing, including automatic speech recognition, speaker identification and verification, and text-to-speech. Existing protocols like SIP and RTSP handle rendezvous and control of media streams but do not cover these special needs. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers that listen to and speak with people need a remote control. This memo lists what that remote control must be able to do.

questions: how do you control a remote speech server
subtitle: Requirements for controlling distributed speech processing services over the network.

tldr.problem: Applications need to use speech processing services (recognizing speech, identifying speakers, generating speech from text) that are distributed on the network, but existing protocols like SIP and RTSP do not adequately address the specific requirements of controlling these services.
tldr.mechanism: The SPEECHSC framework outlines comprehensive requirements for a protocol to control network-based ASR, speaker identification/verification, and TTS servers, covering areas like media handling, grammar support, session parameters, and simultaneous operation of multiple services.
tldr.outcome: This informational document establishes the foundation for designing protocols to manage distributed speech services, enabling applications like VoIP systems, interactive voice response (IVR) platforms, and IP phones to leverage remote speech processing capabilities.

today: RFC 4313 is an informational document that established requirements for the design of SPEECHSC protocols. These requirements influenced the development of MRCP (Media Resource Control Protocol), a real-world protocol for controlling distributed speech resources.

sections.title: Introduction to Distributed Speech Services
sections.content:
Today's multimedia applications benefit from having speech processing available as a distributed network resource. Three categories of speech processing are most important: automatic speech recognition (ASR, which listens to speech and understands what was said), speaker identification and verification (SI/SV, which recognizes who is speaking), and text-to-speech (TTS, which generates spoken audio from text).

While existing protocols like SIP and RTSP handle session setup and media control, they do not address the special requirements of speech processing. This document outlines what a speech control framework (SPEECHSC) must be able to do so that applications like VoIP gateways, interactive voice response systems, and IP phones can control remote speech servers efficiently.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers have different ways to talk to remote services on the network. Some ways work for playing music or movies, but they do not work well for speech processing. This document says what a new way needs to do.

sections.title: The SPEECHSC Architecture
sections.content:
The SPEECHSC framework defines three main network elements. An Application Server decides what transformations to make to media. A Media Processing Entity handles the actual media (this might be a VoIP gateway or a voice browser). An ASR, SI/SV, and/or TTS Server performs the speech processing and either generates audio output (for TTS) or returns recognition results (for ASR and SI/SV).

These elements communicate with each other via SPEECHSC as a control protocol. The framework allows flexible deployment: all elements may run on separate hardware, or multiple elements may reside on the same platform. An RTP stream carries the media separately from the SPEECHSC control protocol. Three examples show how this works in practice: a VoIP gateway using TTS to speak error messages to a caller; a voice browser using ASR to understand caller input; and an IP phone using speaker verification to log the user in.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a restaurant with three parts: the kitchen that makes the food, the waiter who takes orders, and the server who decides what orders to send to which kitchen. SPEECHSC is how they talk to each other.

sections.title: Core Requirements
sections.content:
The SPEECHSC framework must meet several general requirements. It MUST reuse existing protocols where possible and MUST NOT change how existing protocols work. It SHOULD support multiple services in parallel on a single media stream, allowing a server to perform ASR and speaker verification simultaneously on the same audio. The framework MUST allow one session to manage many RTP channels: for example, outbound audio for TTS, inbound for ASR, and another inbound for speaker identification.

The framework MUST be efficient, reusing connections across sessions and caching state where it helps. It MUST support location and load balancing so that clients can find the right server. The framework must address the needs of users with disabilities, such as people who cannot use speech as an interface, and it MUST be able to identify which speech process produced the output (so that audio can be labeled as coming from TTS, ASR, or other services).
sections.plainLanguage: The control system must be fair to everyone, work fast, let multiple jobs run at once, find the right computer to do the work, and tell you what job created what answer.

sections.title: Text-to-Speech Requirements
sections.content:
A TTS server must be able to accept text in multiple formats and render it as audio. It MUST support plain text, and MUST support SSML (Speech Synthesis Markup Language), a standard XML format that lets clients specify voice properties and provide fine control over pronunciation, language, and prosody.

Text may be embedded in the control protocol or referenced by a URI. The client must be able to specify the document type so the server knows how to parse the text. The framework MUST support VCR controls for playback (pause, resume, jump forward or backward by time, words, or sentences). It MUST support speech markers that mark points in the text and send notifications when those points are reached during playback. The framework MUST support session parameters such as language, voice characteristics, and speech rate.
sections.plainLanguage: The system must understand different kinds of text, let you control playback like pause and rewind, and let you mark special spots in the text and get a notification when they are spoken.

sections.title: Speech Recognition and Speaker Identification
sections.content:
ASR clients must be able to request that a server listen to an RTP stream and return recognition results. The framework assumes all ASR servers support SRGS (Voice XML Speech Recognition Grammar Specification), an XML standard for describing what speech the server should recognize. Grammar can be sent by value (embedded) or by reference (as a URI). The client must explicitly specify the grammar format, and the framework SHOULD allow reuse of large grammars across sessions.

Speaker identification and verification (SI/SV) clients request that a server identify or verify a speaker from an RTP stream and return the result. The framework must support identifiers for each verification resource and permit control by ID, because voiceprint formats are vendor-specific. The framework MUST work with servers that maintain state across multiple utterances (for multi-step verification). Both ASR and SI/SV must support input capture so the server can record the media for later analysis and tuning.
sections.plainLanguage: The system must understand what someone is saying and who they are, let you teach it what words to listen for, remember information across multiple spoken phrases, and keep a copy of the audio for later study.

sections.title: Advanced Operations and Security
sections.content:
Interactive systems often need barge-in: the ability for a user to interrupt TTS playback or other prompts by speaking. This requires full-duplex operation, where ASR and TTS run simultaneously on the same connection. Multiple services must be able to run in parallel, for example to perform both ASR and speaker verification on the same utterance, which is the only way to support dynamic challenge phrases (e.g., 'say 51723').

Security considerations are substantial because speech processing may handle sensitive information (financial data, account numbers, voiceprints). The SPEECHSC protocol MUST support authentication, authorization, and integrity, and SHOULD support confidentiality. The protocol may employ existing security machinery like TLS for the control channel and SRTP for media. Voice print databases must be protected against access and misuse. If SI/SV is used for authentication, special care is needed: voiceprints can theoretically be stolen or replayed, and compromised voiceprints cannot be revoked like a password.
sections.plainLanguage: The system must let people interrupt a prompt by speaking, handle many jobs at once, and keep sensitive information like voice patterns locked up safely.
